Relative to the 20-country export basket, its exports are specialised in rare earths (RCA 6636.7).

The DFC and EXIM records show US$372 m of documented commitments from US institutions to Paraguay over 2008–2026 (64 events).

The lenders with the largest recorded commitments to named recipients here are OPIC (predecessor of DFC) (US$232 m), US International Development Finance Corporation (US$101 m) and People's Bank of China (PBC) (US$68 m).
In the UN General Assembly, voting agreement in 2024 was 61% with China and 55% with the United States.
Since 2019, agreement with China fell by 22.8 points and agreement with the United States rose by 29.2 points.
Too few mineral-related legislative records naming either actor have been scored for a stance series (five per year are needed); the text model is zero-shot baseline, not yet validated.

human.title: Paraguay: a balanced index with almost no minerals behind it
human.author: AI-drafted from the site's indicators; not yet reviewed by the project owner
human.text_md:
## Alignment

Paraguay is the only country whose index is balanced: 20.3 for China and 20.1 for the United States in 2024 [index_value:influence:CN:2024] [index_value:influence:US:2024]. There is almost no mineral trade behind either number: the reported mineral exports of 2025 are a few tens of thousands of dollars of rare-earth items, with no reported flow to either power [concentration:share_cn_x:2025]. The money is American: US$349 m of DFC and EXIM commitments in 2015–2021 against US$68 m of Chinese commitments, the only country besides Colombia where the US record is the larger [flow_finance:US:PRY:2015-2021] [flow_finance:CN:PRY:2015-2021]. The four Paraguayan statements in the dataset take no coded position on either power, and no legislative record or headline is coded [coverage:PRY] [statement:count:PRY]. My reading: Paraguay's balance is the arithmetic of UN votes and small loans in a country that recognises Taiwan and exports no minerals to speak of; it says nothing yet about minerals.

## Trajectory

The US index rose 15.1 points over the five years to 2024, the largest rise after Uruguay's and Argentina's, from 4.9 in 2019 (it was 12.1 in 2000 and 3.5 in 2008); the Chinese index fell 4.1 points; in 2025 the US value drops to 0.2 because the UN-voting component, whose source ends in 2024, is not in it [index_value:influence:US:2024] [index_value:influence:CN:2024] [index_value:influence:US:2025]. No flag is raised; the event windows exist but move on a base of a few hundred thousand dollars (−67 points toward the United States after the 2022 US measures, placebo p 0.33), so they say nothing [anomaly_flag:PRY] [event_effect:us_inflation_reduction_act:US:window:PRY].

## Risks and likely next moves

The models forecast the index only (China 19.0 and the United States 0.3 in 2030 at baseline, the US path anchored on the 2025 value without UN voting) and no export share, because the China share has one reported year in its latest unbroken run (2013) and the US share four (2022–2025), fewer than the eight the model needs [forecast:influence_index:CN:baseline:2030:PRY] [forecast:influence_index:US:baseline:2030:PRY] [forecast:export_share:CN:PRY]. In my reading the next move is exploration: the government's interest in rare earths, uranium and lithium is in the statements (uranium takes three of the five mineral mentions) and the press but produces no trade row, and the first offtake agreement would decide which power the minerals, if any, go to [insights:talk_vs_trade_minerals:PRY].

## What would change this reading

A reported mineral export row of any size; a Chinese commitment above the 2015 level; or statements by Paraguayan officials that take a position on either power.
